item.title: Urea offers in India tender fall nearly 10%, offering relief to farmers
item.description: Urea import prices fall nearly 10% from August, offering relief to Indian farmers and potentially easing the government's fertiliser subsidy burden ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: India, a major fertilizer importer, received offers in a urea tender nearly 10% below its August purchase price, signaling some relief for global farmers who have faced surging input costs this year.  Indian Potash Ltd., which also imports urea on behalf of the government, received offers for the west coast between $356.25 and $416.50 a ton in a tender that closed Wednesday, according to traders with direct knowledge of the tender. Offers for supplies to the east coast ranged between $352.10 and $465 a ton, they said.  In both regions, the total volume offered was more than double the amount the agency is seeking. India’s purchases are closely watched as a price benchmark for other importers, who have faced volatile costs this year after the war in Iran curbed the vital Middle Eastern supply. The country paid as much as $959 a ton for urea when the conflict began earlier this year. Prices have since plunged as supply constraints eased while global demand weakened. In its last tender in August, the South Asian nation bought supplies at $390.25 to $393.65 a ton. The decline could signal some relief for farmers worldwide, who are grappling with expensive costs for other key inputs, such as diesel. In India, farmers are preparing to sow crops like wheat, rapeseed and chickpeas in the approaching winter planting season, boosting demand for urea, a key nitrogen-based nutrient needed for crop growth. Lower import prices could also reduce pressure on the government’s fertilizer subsidy bill. A fertilizer ministry spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: US, Russia discuss Nord Stream gas flows to Europe amid Ukraine war
item.description: US and Russian officials discuss bringing a US investor into Nord Stream pipelines, raising the prospect of renewed Russian gas flows to Europe after the Ukraine war.
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / US, Russia discuss Nord Stream gas flows to Europe amid Ukraine war

US, Russia discuss Nord Stream gas flows to Europe amid Ukraine war US and Russian officials discuss bringing a US investor into Nord Stream pipelines, raising the prospect of renewed Russian gas flows to Europe after the Ukraine war.

Talks between Moscow and Washington are taking place against a backdrop of deep European mistrust of Russia's motives

Reuters 5 min read Last Updated : Oct 08 2026 | 10:55 PM IST

Top Russian and US officials, including US Special Envoy Jared Kushner, have held talks about bringing a US investor into the Nord Stream pipelines that delivered gas to Germany before Russia invaded Ukraine, five people with knowledge of the situation said.   The discussions included Kirill Dmitriev, a close adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, the people said.   Kushner, who has been trying to broker a truce between Russia and Ukraine, views doing business as central to restoring peace. Such a deal would enable US investors to profit from energy flows to Europe once the war ends.

Dmitriev and Kushner have met in Moscow and New York in recent weeks. While it was unclear to what degree they discussed Nord Stream on those occasions, the topic remains on the agenda, two of the people told Reuters.   "Any deals will have to be negotiated by Russia with DFC (US International Development Finance Corporation) and Treasury and must benefit United States taxpayers and companies," a White House official said, when asked about the pipeline discussions. Also Read

Ukraine grapples with shortage of troops at front after over 4 years of war

23 Indians rescued after oil tanker attacked off Russia's Black Sea coast

A spy's guide to fighting AI-driven propaganda and disinformation

Exporters to get an extra year on methane rules: EU's Ursula von der Leyen

Kautilya Conclave: Need multi-alignment to navigate world, says Jaishankar

There had been "no Nord Stream discussions recently", the official told Reuters.   Dmitriev, who has campaigned for a resumption of Russian gas sales to Germany, met last month with US Energy and Treasury Department representatives to discuss potential US-Russia energy initiatives. A representative for Dmitriev declined to comment.

It remains unclear how interested Washington is in pursuing the restarting of Russian gas flows to Germany, which is Europe's biggest energy consumer.   A US official said that given the obstacles, a deal is unlikely in the medium term. The Nord Stream gas pipelines are sanctioned by the US and the EU, making any restart illegal.   Trump could waive or soften US sanctions, but if Democrats win control of Congress in next month's midterm elections, this would become harder.   Germany and other European countries, which are spending billions of euros rebuilding their military to defend themselves from Russia, would strongly resist reopening Nord Stream.

A spokeswoman for Germany's economy and energy ministry said Nord Stream and Russian gas were sanctioned in Europe and that Germany had found alternatives. She said any reopening of the pipelines required government approval and this was not desired.   Before Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Germany bought more than half of its gas from Russia through the two Nord Stream pipelines. They were mothballed after Moscow throttled supply to Europe and were blown up in a series of underwater explosions in September 2022.   NORD STREAM OWNERSHIP HURDLES   Talks between Moscow and Washington are taking place against a backdrop of deep European mistrust of Russia's motives.

Earlier this year, the heads of five European spy agencies told Reuters that Russia did not want to end the war quickly and was using US talks to push for business deals instead.   Relations between Russia and Germany, which is among the biggest providers of military support to Ukraine, have hit a low ebb, as officials in Berlin have accused Russia of mounting a systematic campaign of hybrid attacks.   Some German lawmakers say that business deals would bolster Moscow as it pursues war with Ukraine.   "This threatens to be a dirty deal that will cost Europe dearly," said Michael Kellner, a lawmaker who was in charge of German energy policy in the aftermath of the Ukraine invasion.

"Americans and Russians will share the profits," he said.   While Germany's coalition government is opposed to restarting the pipeline, Alternative for Germany (AfD), the country's most popular political party, wants to do so.   Dmitriev will meet the AfD leadership early next year to discuss selling Russian gas again.   But selling ownership of the company that controls the Nord Stream gas pipelines to a US investor or restarting Russian gas faces hurdles.   The company is 51% owned by Russian state energy giant Gazprom, with a further 31% split between two German entities and the rest in the hands of a French and a Dutch firm.

The two German shareholders are seeking to keep their shares to maintain German influence, should Gazprom sell its stake, said another person.   Days after the Moscow meetings, Kushner said in Kyiv he had spoken to European counterparts about how the war pushed up energy prices, advocating "prosperity agreements" to encourage peace and give "leaders ... something to look forward to".   While a gas deal would please the Kremlin, it would split German public opinion, which is divided over buying Russian energy, and Europe, where Poland and the Baltic states are particularly vulnerable to Russia and reject energy ties.   Poland's political leadership is watching the discussions to reopen the pipeline but remains firmly opposed, said one person with knowledge of the government's thinking.

Kushner and Dmitriev have also been discussing the sale of a collection of businesses, from oil refineries to petrol stations in Europe and elsewhere which are owned by Russian energy company Lukoil, said two other people familiar with the matter.   Under that plan, a consortium of the DFC federal investment agency and investors from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates would buy the assets, while US authorities would lift sanctions, those people said.   "On Lukoil, Steve (Witkoff) and Jared (Kushner) worked with DFC to negotiate a substantial upfront payment and profits interest for the United States," said a White House official.   Lukoil and Gazprom did not respond to requests for comment.

item.title: Govt counters Musk, says satellite clearance process non-discriminatory
item.description: India’s communications ministry on Thursday said it followed a “fair and non-discriminatory” authorisation framework for all telecommunication services, including satellite communication services, and ...
item.dc:creator: Gulveen Aulakh
item.content:encoded: Even as India’s communications ministry on Thursday said it was following a “fair and non-discriminatory” authorisation framework for all telecommunications services, including those related to satellite communication (satcom), Elon Musk, the founder of SpaceX and Tesla, questioned the absence of a licence to Starlink through a post on X. “Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license? Is Ambani the real boss of India?” the American billionaire posted on the social media platform X, which he owns. Earlier in the day, the Indian government had reiterated that preferential clearance for any single operator would be inconsistent with India’s regulatory environment. “At present, all the three entities are at broadly the same regulatory stage. As such, the suggestion that the framework or its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived,” the communications ministry said. The ministry’s statement came a day after Musk alleged that “certain oligarchs” were blocking his satellite internet company’s entry into India. “Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people. You can guess who they are… This is a crime against the people of India!” Musk said in a post on X late Wednesday evening, without then naming any company or group. His response was to a post by @DogeDesigner that said India needed Starlink because of its ability to offer connectivity to the remotest regions of the country, and that the government should complete the remaining clearances and spectrum allocation. “Indian needs Starlink. 11,256 of India’s listed villages still had no 4G coverage as of May 2026… BharatNet has laid more than 850,000 route-kilometre of fibre and made about 221,000 gram panchayats (GPs) service-ready. Yet its points of presence were reported operational at only 80,472 GPs as of June 2026…,” the DogeDesigner post said. Starlink is among three applicants seeking to offer satellite broadband services in India. The other two are Bharti group-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, now part of Eutelsat Group, and Reliance Industries-backed Jio Satellite Communications, a subsidiary of Reliance Jio. All three have been awarded licences but are awaiting security clearances. Jio is separately building its own low-Earth orbit (Leo) satellite constellation, which will rival global players such as Starlink and Amazon Leo (formerly known as Project Kuiper), the latter of which is also eyeing an entry into India.Starlink received its last approvals last year, while Eutelsat and Jio received theirs earlier. The Department of Telecommunications has approved a spectrum charge of 5 per cent of adjusted gross revenue, which is yet to be approved by the Union Cabinet. Commercial launches by any of the companies would be dependent on government approvals and clearances, which are yet to be granted. India is seeking assurances of control over the satellite systems in case of exigencies, according to people aware of the developments. Musk’s post came hours after Lauren Dreyer, vice-president, business operations, SpaceX, said the company was ready for the Indian market as soon as the country gave it the green signal. She added that the firm had built its operations specifically for India’s security requirements. “We are standing ready to serve India once India is ready. We’re ready to work with the government. We are ready to work with operators and with industry to this end. We are ready to help Prime Minister Narendra Modi achieve his vision of 100 per cent connectivity throughout India — a vision all of our company, including Elon, shares,” Dreyer said at the India Mobile Congress on Wednesday. “Hopefully, next time I address the Congress, the government’s work will be complete, and Starlink will be authorised and ready,” she said. Starlink is awaiting security clearance and approval for foreign direct investment from the government, having received permissions from the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre and a Global Mobile Personal Communications by Satellite licence. Dreyer said Starlink had already made investments in India, with more than 20 gateway sites ready to begin operations.The company was also ensuring that its business met the security requirements and other regulations needed to operate in the country, she said. Dreyer observed that Starlink had been building relationships with industry, including tieups with Bharti Airtel and Jio, and partnering state governments over the past five years to better understand the market and prepare for the start of operations. “We have built our Starlink operations specifically for India in recognition of Indian security requirements and other regulations, establishing controls at every layer for India and keeping Indian user data within India. We have already made the investment and built the existing ground infrastructure here — 20 gateway sites comprising hundreds of antennae — and we have established the operations to be ready to serve India,” she said. She also said that the digital divide must be narrowed and that this would not be possible by leaving out a substantial portion of the population. “But there’s no one of us that can solve this challenging problem of the digital divide. It takes all of us thinking about how to apply the best technology in the places that it serves best. As Starlink serves over 170 countries around the world and growing, our consistent theme has been to work very closely with governments, private industry, and all of those looking to connect people who need reliable connectivity and connect and connected around the world,” she added. Terming India’s achievements in digital connectivity “extraordinary”, with millions connected and affordable data available at scale, Dreyer flagged that the last mile remained. “It’s the most challenging to connect. It’s also where Starlink offers the biggest potential to help accelerate the speed to connect 100 per cent of India. With Starlink, people can get connected within minutes, not years,” she added.

item.title: Govt says satellite internet rules fair after Musk's Starlink bias claim
item.description: The government says all three licensed satellite communication providers are undergoing security assessments and must meet the same regulatory requirements before receiving spectrum ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / News / Govt says satellite internet rules fair after Musk's Starlink bias claim

Govt says satellite internet rules fair after Musk's Starlink bias claim The government says all three licensed satellite communication providers are undergoing security assessments and must meet the same regulatory requirements before receiving spectrum

The government's clarification comes a day after Starlink said it had already invested in infrastructure and established security controls specifically designed to comply with Indian regulations | Image: Bloomberg

Our Bureau New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 08 2026 | 9:48 AM IST

Listen to This Article

The Union government on Thursday rejected allegations of discrimination in India's satellite communication regulatory framework, a day after billionaire Elon Musk claimed that certain "oligarchs" were blocking the launch of his satellite internet company Starlink in the country.   A statement issued by the Ministry of Communications said it had established a fair and non-discriminatory authorisation framework for all telecommunications services, including satellite communications.   The clarification came after Musk alleged on social media platform X on Wednesday that unnamed business interests were preventing Starlink from entering the Indian market to protect their existing dominance.   "Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people. You can guess who they are… This is a crime against the people of India!" Musk said in his post. He did not name any company or individual.     Responding to the allegations, the government said suggestions that its regulatory framework or its implementation was discriminatory were "baseless and misconceived". Also Read

Musk blames 'certain oligarchs' for delay in Starlink's entry into India

SpaceX in talks with investors to borrow $40 billion to buy Nvidia chips

Elon Musk is a trillionaire again as SpaceX claws back post-IPO slump

Elon Musk to rename SpaceX AI arm SpaceXSI after Trump's directive

Elon Musk warns Delta Air Lines CEO 'will lose his job' over Starlink snub

What did the government say about Starlink's India approvals? The Ministry of Communications said licences had been granted to three providers offering Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite (GMPCS) services using non-geosynchronous satellite orbit systems.   These include Musk-owned Starlink, Bharti Group-backed Eutelsat OneWeb and Reliance Industries-backed Jio Satellite Communications.   Under the licensing conditions, every operator must demonstrate compliance with security requirements before proceeding to the next stage of regulatory approval.   "Security assessment as part of this process is currently under way in respect of all the three licensees," the ministry said.   It added that the assessments were intended to ensure the safety of users and their data.   Once a licensed entity completes the security assessment, it can proceed to seek spectrum assignment.   "At present, all the three entities are at broadly the same regulatory stage," the government said, dismissing suggestions of preferential treatment or discrimination. Why has Starlink's India launch been delayed? Starlink has been seeking to enter the Indian market since November 2022 but has faced several regulatory hurdles, particularly relating to security clearance and foreign direct investment approval.   The company received a GMPCS licence from the Department of Telecommunications in June 2025, followed by authorisation from the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) in July 2025.   However, the company is still awaiting the remaining approvals required to begin commercial operations. What has Starlink said about its readiness to launch in India? The government's clarification comes a day after Starlink said it had already invested in infrastructure and established security controls specifically designed to comply with Indian regulations.   Speaking at the India Mobile Congress on Wednesday, Lauren Dreyer, vice-president of Starlink business operations at SpaceX, said the company had built 20 gateway sites comprising hundreds of antennas in India.   She said Starlink had also established safeguards to ensure that Indian user data remained within the country. "We have built our Starlink operations specifically for India in recognition of Indian security requirements and other regulations, establishing controls at every layer for India and keeping Indian user data within India," Dreyer said.   The company has also established partnerships with Bharti Airtel and Reliance Jio as part of its preparations to enter the market. Dreyer said Starlink was ready to begin providing services once the government completed the necessary approval process.   "We are standing ready to serve India once India is ready," she said.
